name: autumn equinox

attributes.attribute: equinoxes and solstices were not celebrated by the ancient Celts
equinoctial feast on or about September 29
date when rents and loans were repaid and contracts settled
the autumn goose harvest, begun at Michaelmas
character in English mummers parades with Robin Hood and the hobby-horse

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The autumn equinox is an astronomical feast. The ancient Celts did not celebrate the equinoxes or the solstices. They kept the fixed points of the solar year instead, namely Imbolc, Beltane, Lughnasa, and Samhain. After the Normans and Christianity arrived in Ireland, an equinoctial feast appeared on or about September 29. This feast of St. Michael the Archangel, or Michaelmas, fixed the date for repaying rents and loans and for settling contracts. Elected officials took and left office on Michaelmas, and harvest fairs often marked the day. Michaelmas opened the Fomhar na nGéan, the goose harvest, when butchering began and farmers were expected to give meat to the poor. In England the autumn equinox brought mummers' parades where Robin Hood and Maid Marion Dance with the hobby-horse. Koch finds no convincing evidence that the Celts celebrated solstices or equinoxes and lists Michaelmas as a quarter day.

okr.objective: Establish that the Celts did not celebrate solstices or equinoxes and that an autumn feast came only with later Christian practice.
key_results: Michaelmas is the equinoctial feast fixed at or about September 29.
Michaelmas dates rents and loans and the settling of contracts.
The autumn season drew the goose harvest, Fomhar na nGéia.
In England autumn fairs few mummers with Robin Hood and Maid Marion.
